context_blurb:
In a desert, a baking afternoon can turn into a chilly night, while a muggy night in the American Southeast stays warm until dawn. The difference is water vapour, a gas that holds in the ground's heat. That warming is called the greenhouse effect.

Much sunlight crosses the air and heats the ground, and the warm ground sends out infrared rays, invisible light that carries heat. A greenhouse gas, such as water vapour or carbon dioxide, absorbs those rays and soon gives the energy off again in any direction, so part of it heads back down to the ground and part goes on toward space. Earth still sends out to space about as much energy as it takes in from sunlight; the gases only slow its escape.

In 1856 Eunice Foote set two identical glass cylinders with thermometers in the sun, one holding carbon dioxide and one plain air. The carbon dioxide grew hotter, reaching 125 degrees Fahrenheit against the air's 106, and once both were back in the shade it stayed hot many times as long. An atmosphere of that gas, she wrote, would give Earth a high temperature. Her cylinders took in all of sunlight, though, not just the heat rays the ground gives off.

In London three years later, John Tyndall tested gases with invisible heat rays alone. He sent heat from a copper cube of hot water down a brass tube to a detector whose needle swung as the heat arrived. Dry air, nitrogen and oxygen barely moved it; their molecules, each a pair of matching atoms, hardly respond to infrared. Air straight from his laboratory stopped far more heat, and most of that was the work of its water vapour, which absorbed at least thirteen times as much as the dry air itself. Carbon dioxide absorbed heat too, but the air holds far less of it.

The Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius was after an old riddle, what had brought on the ice ages, for no one could explain how Earth had grown cold enough for one. With Samuel Langley's readings of the Moon's invisible heat, he worked out by hand, in thousands of calculations he called tedious, published in 1896, how each band of latitude would warm or cool as the air's carbon dioxide rose or fell. A deep enough cut in the gas, he calculated, would cool the middle latitudes enough, he thought, for an ice age.

Many 1950s scientists expected the sea to swallow nearly all the carbon dioxide from burning coal and oil. In 1958, on the bare lava of Mauna Loa, a Hawaiian volcano far out at sea, Charles David Keeling started measuring the gas. His first reading was 313 parts per million: 313 molecules in every million molecules of air. By 1960 his readings showed the gas building up from one year to the next. It has risen every year since.

Keeling's line also zigzags, dipping each year between May and October and rising again until the next May. Most of Earth's land, and so most of its plants, lies in the northern half of the world. Through the northern spring and summer, forests and fields take carbon dioxide from the air as they grow, and in autumn and winter their dead leaves and plants decay and give it back. The southern half has far less land, and at the South Pole the swing almost vanishes.

Plants take carbon from the air, breathing and decay return it, the sea dissolves it, and burning coal, oil and gas, the fossil fuels made from long-buried life, returns their ancient carbon to the air. Leave aside the carbon locked away in rock, and the greatest store is the oceans, with about 38,000 billion tonnes dissolved in sea water, some forty to fifty times as much as the air holds.

Volcanoes can cool the world instead. In April 1815 Mount Tambora, in Indonesia, blew apart in the most powerful eruption ever recorded, and its cloud reached the stratosphere, the layer of air above the weather. There Tambora's sulfur gas, some sixty million tonnes of sulfur dioxide, turned into a haze of tiny droplets of sulfuric acid, which reflected sunlight back into space for a year or more. Ash cannot do that, since it falls out of the sky within days or weeks. So 1816 was the year without a summer, with June snow in New England and failed harvests across Europe.
